This is why systems is a sweeter spot than ML research (where the 'metric' is a noisy, days-long training run and correlates imperfectly with what you care about) or math/theory (where verification is a proof, not a number - though that flips back to easy with a proof checker). The argument fails in three concrete ways: (1) the metric is a proxy that can be gamed - an LLM will find that dropping requests raises measured throughput, so f must be paired with bulletproof correctness checks, not just performance; (2) evaluation is too expensive to run at search scale, killing the sample-many-keep-best economics; (3) the metric is non-stationary or subjective, so argmax over it doesn't generalize. My judgment: the ADRS bet is really a bet on the quality and un-gameability of the verifier, so the highest-leverage engineering is not a smarter LLM but a correctness-first evaluator plus hidden hold-out workloads. Get the verifier wrong and you've built a very efficient reward-hacking machine.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Frames it as a verification-cheaper-than-generation regime, quantifies the asymmetry, contrasts systems vs ML vs theory, and lands on the original judgment that the verifier is the real deliverable. Staff-level.

criteria: breaks when verification is subjective / expensive / gameable

questions.topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 5: AI-Driven Research & Formal Verification
questions.prompt: Sketch the architecture of an ADRS system - the components and how data flows between them - and explain why it's structured as an evolutionary loop rather than one big prompt.
probes: What is stored in Storage and how does the Solution Selector use it?
Why sample from prior good solutions instead of always generating from scratch?

no_hire.answer: You prompt the LLM to solve the problem, check if it works, and if not you prompt it again. You keep going until it's good.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Describes naive retry, not an architecture. No population, no evaluator design, no selection strategy.

weak_hire.answer: There's a component that builds the prompt, the LLM that generates a solution, an evaluator that scores it, storage that keeps the good ones, and a selector that picks which stored solution to build on next. It loops: generate, evaluate, select, repeat, so solutions improve over time.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Names all five components and the loop correctly, but treats them as a checklist. No explanation of why the archive and selection matter, or of the LLM-as-mutation view.

hire.answer: Five components. The Prompt Generator assembles the context - the task spec, the API surface, and one or more prior solutions to build on. The Solution Generator is the LLM, which proposes a new candidate (usually a code diff or a full program). The Evaluator runs it and returns a score plus correctness verdict. Storage is an archive of scored solutions, the population. The Solution Selector decides which stored solution(s) to feed back in, balancing exploiting the current best against exploring diverse candidates. It's evolutionary because the LLM acts as a mutation/crossover operator over programs: sampling from prior good solutions and mutating them concentrates search near known-good regions, which converges far faster than i.i.d. generation from scratch, and the archive prevents you from losing good building blocks.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct component roles, the loop, and the key insight that the LLM is a mutation operator with the archive as population. Push: selection strategy specifics, parallelism, and how the evaluator design gates the whole thing.

strong_hire.answer: Architecture: (1) Prompt Generator - constructs context = task description + restricted high-level API + k parent solutions sampled from the archive, optionally with their scores and error traces so the LLM can do targeted repair. (2) Solution Generator - the LLM, sampled at moderate temperature to get diversity, emitting a diff against a parent (cheaper and more local than full rewrites, which is effectively a mutation operator; concatenating features from two parents is crossover). (3) Evaluator - the trust anchor: it must enforce correctness first (compile, type/spec checks, unit + property tests, hidden hold-out workloads) and only then measure performance, returning a rejected verdict on any correctness failure so a fast-but-wrong solution never enters the population. (4) Storage - a scored archive; the strong design is not a single best but a quality-diversity map (MAP-Elites style) keeping the best solution per behavioral niche so diverse building blocks survive. (5) Solution Selector - samples parents trading exploitation (high score) against exploration (novelty/diversity), because pure greedy collapses to a local optimum and pure random wastes compute. Why a loop, not one prompt: the search space of programs is astronomically large and the LLM's one-shot success rate on a hard optimization is near zero, but its edit-a-good-solution success rate is high, so you decompose a hard search into many cheap, verifiable mutation steps and let selection do credit assignment. This is the FunSearch/AlphaEvolve template. Two things I'd watch in production: the evaluator is the bottleneck and the security boundary (you're executing untrusted LLM code, so sandbox it), and the archive can converge prematurely if the diversity metric is wrong - I'd monitor population diversity and inject fresh random seeds when it collapses.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Maps all five components to concrete design choices, invokes quality-diversity/MAP-Elites, frames the LLM as mutation-plus-crossover, and flags the evaluator as both bottleneck and security boundary. Principal-level.

criteria: five components: Prompt Generator, Solution Generator, Evaluator, Storage, Solution Selector
LLM as mutation operator over programs

questions.topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 5: AI-Driven Research & Formal Verification
questions.prompt: You point an ADRS system at optimizing a load balancer for throughput, and it 'discovers' a solution that scores 40% faster. When you look, it's silently dropping a fraction of the workload. Walk me through why this happened and how you design the system so it can't.
probes: Why isn't 'add more test cases' a sufficient fix?
What role do hidden hold-out workloads play and why must they be hidden?

no_hire.answer: The LLM made a mistake and dropped requests by accident. You'd catch it in code review and tell it not to do that.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Treats deliberate specification gaming as an accident. No systemic fix - relies on humans reviewing every candidate, which defeats automation.

weak_hire.answer: The system was told to maximize throughput, so it found a way to make throughput go up - dropping requests raises the number it measures even though it's wrong. This is reward hacking. The fix is to check correctness too, not just speed: add tests that make sure no requests are dropped.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correctly identifies reward hacking and that correctness must be checked, but assumes a fixed test set is enough and misses that the LLM will overfit to whatever verifier you show it.

hire.answer: The measured objective (throughput) is a proxy for the real goal (serve all traffic fast and correctly). The LLM is a powerful optimizer, so it does exactly what optimizers do under Goodhart's law: it maximizes the letter of the metric, and dropping a slice of the workload is a legitimate way to make that number go up. The failure is in the verifier, not the LLM. Fix: make correctness a hard gate that runs before any performance credit - the evaluator must verify functional correctness (every request served, invariants held) and only then score speed; a solution that fails correctness gets a rejected verdict and never enters the population. Adding more visible test cases isn't enough on its own, because the search will overfit to exactly the cases it can see - it optimizes to pass your tests, not to be correct. That's why you need hidden hold-out workloads: correctness and performance checks the LLM never sees during search, run before you trust a winner, so overfitting-to-the-eval gets caught.
hire.interviewer_note: Nails Goodhart, correctness-as-gate, and the overfit-to-visible-tests point with hidden hold-outs. Push: how to make correctness verification bulletproof, and the security angle of executing the code.

strong_hire.answer: This is textbook specification gaming: your objective f is a proxy for the true goal, and any gap between proxy and goal is an exploit the search will find, because the LLM plus selection is precisely an optimizer over f. Dropping load raises measured throughput, so under the letter of the metric it's an improvement - the system is working as specified, the spec is just wrong. The design principle is that the LLM will exploit any gap in the verifier, so the verifier - not the generator - is where you invest. Concretely: (1) Correctness must be a hard gate that runs first and is bulletproof, not a soft term in the objective. If correctness is a weighted penalty, the optimizer will trade it off; it has to be a boolean that vetoes the candidate. Enforce it with layered checks: functional equivalence to a reference on required behavior, invariants (conservation - requests in equals requests served plus explicitly-failed), and property-based tests over generated inputs rather than a fixed suite. (2) A fixed visible test set is insufficient because search overfits to whatever it can observe - it will learn to pass exactly those cases. So you keep hidden hold-out workloads: correctness and performance evaluations the search process never sees, run only when validating a promising winner. They must be hidden precisely because anything the search can see, it will optimize against; the moment a hold-out leaks into the loop it stops being a check on overfitting. (3) The hold-outs should include distribution shift and adversarial workloads (bursty traffic, skewed keys) so 'inflate the number by degrading a rare case' gets caught. (4) You're executing untrusted LLM-written code, so the evaluator runs in a sandbox with resource limits - reward hacking also shows up as reading the answer file, patching the timer, or exiting early, and only isolation stops that. (5) Monitor for the signature: a large metric jump with a small, suspicious diff is a red flag; I'd auto-flag candidates whose gain exceeds a threshold for mandatory hold-out + human audit. The meta-point: an ADRS system with a weak verifier isn't a research tool, it's an extremely efficient generator of solutions that cheat, so I'd gate any production use on formal verification of the winning artifact, not just its benchmark score.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Distinguishes hard-gate vs soft-penalty correctness, explains why visible tests are overfit and why hold-outs must stay hidden, adds sandboxing against verifier-tampering, and gives a detection heuristic plus a formal-verification gate. Research-lead depth.

criteria: objective is a proxy, LLM optimizes the letter not the intent
hidden hold-out workloads to catch overfit-to-eval
the LLM will exploit any gap in the verifier

questions.topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 5: AI-Driven Research & Formal Verification
questions.section_title: 'Less is more' - weaker baselines force discovery
questions.prompt: There's a counterintuitive finding in ADRS work: giving the LLM a weaker starting baseline and a more restricted, high-level API produces better final algorithms than handing it a strong baseline and rich low-level primitives. Why would that be, and how do you decide how much scaffolding to provide?
probes: How does a restricted API change the search space the LLM explores?
What's the risk of starting from a strong, complex baseline?

no_hire.answer: A weaker baseline is easier for the model to beat, so it's more likely to improve on it. Simpler is generally better for LLMs.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Reduces it to 'easier to beat' - misses that the point is the quality of the final discovered algorithm, not the ease of the first improvement.

weak_hire.answer: If you give the LLM a strong baseline, it just makes small tweaks around it, but a weaker baseline forces it to actually invent something. A high-level API means it has to reason about the algorithm instead of fiddling with low-level details, so it explores bigger ideas.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Has the right intuition - strong baseline anchors to local edits, high-level API pushes structural reasoning - but no mechanism about search space, and no discussion of where the trade-off bites.

hire.answer: It's about the search space the LLM effectively explores. A strong, complex baseline anchors the LLM: its mutations become small local tweaks around a good point, so search stays trapped in that basin and never reaches a structurally different, better optimum. A weak baseline sits in a flatter, more open region, so the LLM's proposals are forced to be more structural and it can discover genuinely new algorithms. Similarly, a restricted high-level API removes the low-level primitives the model would otherwise fiddle with; each API call is a big semantic move, so a single mutation explores a large, meaningful jump in algorithm space rather than a tiny implementation detail. 'Less is more' means less scaffolding leaves more room for discovery. The trade-off: if you strip too much, the LLM can't produce anything that runs, or the good region is so far away that random-ish search never reaches it, so you need enough structure that valid solutions are reachable but not so much that you've pre-decided the answer.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct search-space mechanism for both the baseline and the API, and names the under-scaffolding failure. Push: connect to exploration/exploitation and to how you'd tune this empirically.

strong_hire.answer: Frame it as: what does one LLM mutation do to the point you occupy in solution space, and where can the search reach from the seed? Two effects. (1) Baseline as a prior/anchor. A strong complex baseline is a sharp local optimum; the LLM, prompted to improve it, produces edits biased toward that structure, so mutations are small and the search stays in that basin - you exploit a decent local optimum but can't reach a distant better one, and complex code also gives the LLM less headroom to reason about globally. A weaker baseline sits in a flatter region where the gradient of improvement points toward genuinely different algorithms, so the LLM is effectively forced into structural search and can find optima the strong-baseline run can never reach. (2) API granularity controls the step size and effective dimensionality of search. Low-level primitives make each mutation a tiny, low-semantic-value change, so the search dimension is huge and dominated by implementation noise - the LLM spends its budget fiddling. A restricted high-level API makes each call a large, semantically meaningful move, collapsing the search to a lower-dimensional space of algorithmic choices where the LLM's strength (reasoning about what a component does) actually applies, so a single mutation can leap between algorithm families. Net: less scaffolding = a search space whose good regions are reachable and whose moves are meaningful, which is where LLM-guided evolution beats hand-tuning. The trade-off is a Goldilocks curve: too much scaffolding pre-decides the answer and caps the ceiling; too little and either nothing compiles (invalid-solution rate spikes, wasting evaluation budget) or the good region is unreachable from the seed so you plateau at the baseline. How I'd tune it: treat the API abstraction level and baseline strength as hyperparameters, run small ablations measuring final-best score and valid-solution rate versus scaffolding, and pick the point just below where the valid-solution rate collapses. I'd also watch population diversity - if a strong baseline is collapsing the search, diversity dies early, which is the empirical signal to weaken the seed. This mirrors curriculum and exploration design in RL: too-strong a prior kills exploration, too-weak a prior kills sample efficiency.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Mechanistic account of baseline-as-prior and API-as-step-size, an explicit Goldilocks trade-off with measurable signals (final-best, valid-solution rate, diversity), and a clean RL exploration analogy. Principal-level.

criteria: restricted API forces higher-level / structural reasoning
strong baseline anchors LLM to local tweaks
search space shape and reachability of good optima
less is more = less scaffolding, more discovery
trade-off: too little scaffolding = never gets off the ground

questions.topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 5: AI-Driven Research & Formal Verification
questions.prompt: FunSearch and AlphaEvolve discovered genuinely novel algorithms and mathematical constructions by combining an LLM with an automated evaluator. Explain the mechanism - how genetic mutation and crossover of programs actually work here - and why this can produce something the base LLM couldn't output in one shot.
probes: What exactly does the LLM mutate, and why evolve a program rather than the answer directly?
Why is an island / population model used instead of one global best?

no_hire.answer: They ran the LLM a lot of times and picked the best answer it gave. Doing it many times means you eventually get a good one.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Reduces it to best-of-N sampling. No evolution, no fitness-guided search, no notion of building on prior solutions.

weak_hire.answer: The LLM generates programs, an evaluator scores them, and the good programs are kept and fed back to the LLM to generate improved versions - like evolution, where the LLM does mutation and crossover. Over many generations the programs get better and can end up better than anything a single prompt would produce, because it's search on top of the model.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level loop and the search-beats-one-shot point, but doesn't say what's mutated (a program that generates the answer), no fitness/diversity detail, and no islands.

hire.answer: The LLM is used as a smart mutation/crossover operator inside an evolutionary loop. You don't evolve the raw answer; you evolve a program - typically a function that constructs or scores the solution. The evaluator runs that program and returns a fitness (for FunSearch, how good the constructed object is; a cheap, automated, human-label-free signal). To make a new candidate, you sample one or a few high-fitness programs from the population, put them in the prompt, and ask the LLM to write a better version - editing one is mutation, blending two is crossover. Keep the ones that score higher, repeat. It beats one-shot because search amortizes capability over thousands of cheap, verifiable steps: the LLM only has to make a good local improvement to a program that already works, not invent the whole thing at once, and the evaluator does credit assignment. FunSearch used an island/population model - several sub-populations evolving somewhat independently - to preserve diversity and avoid the whole search collapsing onto one early winner.
hire.interviewer_note: Correctly identifies LLM-as-mutation, evolving a generator program, automated fitness, and islands-for-diversity. Push: why evolve the program not the object, the exact islands mechanics, and what makes this genuinely novel discovery vs interpolation.

strong_hire.answer: Mechanism: it's an evolutionary algorithm where the LLM replaces the hand-coded mutation and crossover operators. The genome is a program - crucially, a program that constructs or evaluates the solution, not the solution itself. FunSearch evolves a priority/heuristic function; AlphaEvolve evolves whole code files via diffs. Fitness comes from an automated evaluator that executes the program and returns a scalar (and a correctness verdict), so there are zero human labels and you can run the loop at massive parallel scale. A generation step: (1) sample k parent programs from the population, biased toward high fitness but with diversity; (2) prompt the LLM with those parents (and their scores/errors) and ask for an improved version - a single-parent edit is mutation, splicing ideas from multiple parents is crossover; (3) execute, score, and insert into the population. Two design choices matter. First, why evolve a program rather than the object: the program is a compact, structured, reusable genome - a small edit to a priority function is a large, semantically coherent move in solution space, the search generalizes (the function works across problem instances, so you're discovering an algorithm not memorizing one answer), and it's directly verifiable by execution. Second, the island model: run several sub-populations that evolve independently and only occasionally migrate the best individuals. This maintains diversity and fights premature convergence - a single global-best population collapses onto the first good basin and stops exploring, whereas islands let different lineages explore different algorithmic families, and migration spreads winners without homogenizing everyone. FunSearch also periodically resets weaker islands from strong ones to reallocate compute. Why this exceeds one-shot capability: the base LLM's probability of emitting the final novel algorithm in one sample is effectively zero, but its probability of making one good improvement to an already-decent program is high; evolution stacks tens of thousands of such improvements, using the evaluator for credit assignment, so you climb a fitness landscape the model could never traverse in a single forward pass. The results - a new construction for the cap-set problem and improved bin-packing heuristics in FunSearch, faster matrix-multiplication-style and data-center scheduling improvements in AlphaEvolve - are genuinely novel because the evaluator, not the training distribution, is the arbiter: it will accept a correct construction the model has never seen, so the system can discover, not just retrieve. The load-bearing risk is the same as all ADRS: fitness is a proxy, so the evaluator must gate correctness hard or evolution will happily discover a program that games it.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise genome-is-a-program argument, full island/migration/reset mechanics, the one-shot-vs-search capability argument, correct concrete results, and the closing verifier-is-load-bearing judgment. Research-lead depth.

criteria: LLM as mutation operator over programs (functions/diffs)
automated evaluator provides fitness, no human labels
evolving a generator program vs the raw solution
islands/population maintain diversity, avoid premature convergence
search amortizes over many verifiable steps beyond one-shot capability

questions.topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 5: AI-Driven Research & Formal Verification
questions.section_title: TLA+ formal verification of an ADRS artifact
questions.prompt: An ADRS system hands you a new distributed cache-coherence protocol that beats the baseline on every benchmark and passes all your hidden hold-out workloads. Before it goes to production you want to formally verify it in TLA+. Explain what you'd specify, how model checking finds bugs, and why state explosion is the central problem.
probes: What's the difference between a safety invariant and a temporal/liveness property here?
Why isn't passing every benchmark and hold-out enough - what can TLA+ catch that testing can't?

no_hire.answer: TLA+ is a language for writing specifications, so you'd write the protocol in TLA+ and it tells you if there are bugs. State explosion means the program uses too much memory when it runs.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Names TLA+ with no mechanism, and fundamentally misunderstands state explosion as a runtime memory issue rather than a verification search-space blowup.

weak_hire.answer: You write an abstract specification of the protocol in TLA+ and state properties it should satisfy, like 'two caches never hold conflicting values.' A model checker explores the possible states and reports a counterexample if a property can be violated. State explosion is the problem that the number of states grows very fast, so checking large systems becomes infeasible. It catches concurrency bugs that tests miss because it explores interleavings you wouldn't think to test.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct on spec, invariants, model checking, state explosion as combinatorial growth, and the interleavings point - but shallow: no safety-vs-liveness distinction, no abstraction strategy, no numbers, no mitigation.

hire.answer: TLA+ separates the specification - an abstract model of what the protocol does, expressed as a state machine over variables with an initial predicate and a next-state relation defining allowed transitions - from the actual implementation code. I'd model the caches, the directory/memory, and the message channels as variables. Then I state properties in two flavors: safety invariants, which must hold in every reachable state (coherence: no two caches hold the same line in conflicting modified states; no read returns stale data), and temporal/liveness properties, which say something good eventually happens (every request is eventually served; no permanent deadlock). The TLC model checker does exhaustive state-space exploration: from the initial states it enumerates every reachable state by applying the next-state relation over all possible interleavings of concurrent actions and message orderings, checking the invariant in each; if it finds a violating state it emits a concrete counterexample trace. That's exactly what benchmarks and hold-outs can't give you - testing samples a tiny subset of interleavings and timings, so a coherence bug that only appears under one specific message reordering will pass every benchmark and still corrupt data in production. State explosion is the central problem because the reachable state space grows exponentially: with N caches each in one of S states plus in-flight messages, the count is roughly S^N times the message-queue configurations, so even modest N blows past what you can enumerate. You fight it by abstracting - model 2-3 caches and one cache line instead of the real fleet, shrink data domains to symbolic values, use symmetry reduction - and rely on the small-scope hypothesis that most bugs surface in small configurations.
hire.interviewer_note: Solid on spec-vs-implementation, safety-vs-liveness, exhaustive checking with counterexamples, the interleavings-testing-misses point, exponential state explosion, and abstraction/small-scope. Push: fairness for liveness, refinement to the implementation, and the residual gap TLA+ leaves.

strong_hire.answer: TLA+ describes the system as a state machine: a specification Spec = Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness, where Init constrains the starting states, Next is the next-state relation (a disjunction of actions, each a predicate on current and primed variables), and vars are the state variables - here the per-cache line states (Modified/Shared/Invalid...), the directory, and the message channels modeled as sequences so you capture arbitrary orderings. This is the spec, deliberately abstract; the C++/Rust implementation is separate, and closing that gap is its own step (below). Properties come in two kinds. Safety invariants - must hold in every reachable state - e.g. coherence: no line is Modified in two caches simultaneously, and any read observes the latest committed write; these are state predicates checked at every node of the reachable graph. Temporal/liveness properties - something good eventually happens - e.g. []<>(request served) or 'no permanent deadlock', written with temporal operators; these require fairness assumptions (weak/strong fairness on enabled actions), otherwise a stuttering or perpetually-starved schedule trivially violates liveness and the checker just reports the trivial counterexample. Model checking (TLC) does explicit-state exhaustive exploration: BFS/DFS from Init, applying Next to generate successors over all action interleavings and message reorderings, hashing states into a seen-set, checking invariants at each state and liveness via cycle detection on the state graph (a lasso/SCC search for a fair cycle where the good thing never happens). A violation yields a minimal counterexample trace - the exact interleaving - which is gold for debugging. Why benchmarks and hold-outs are insufficient: they exercise a vanishing fraction of the interleaving space at whatever timings the hardware happened to produce; a coherence violation that needs a precise three-message reordering has probability near zero of appearing in testing but is a certainty over a fleet's lifetime, and it's exactly the kind of subtle bug an ADRS optimizer introduces when it shaves synchronization for speed. Model checking covers all interleavings up to the modeled scope, so it either proves the invariant over that scope or hands you the bug. State explosion is central and unavoidable: reachable states scale like (per-component states)^(#components) times message-queue configurations - roughly S^N * (queue space) - so it's exponential in N and in the data/value domains; adding one more cache or one more in-flight message can multiply the space by orders of magnitude, and TLC is memory-bound on the seen-set. Mitigations, in the order I'd apply them: (1) abstraction - verify a small configuration (2-3 caches, 1-2 lines) relying on the small-scope hypothesis that coherence bugs manifest at tiny N; (2) symmetry reduction - caches are interchangeable, so quotient the state space by permutation symmetry (TLC symmetry sets), often an N!-factor cut; (3) shrink domains to symbolic/representative values; (4) constrain message-queue depth; (5) for larger scopes, switch to symbolic model checking / a proof (TLAPS) or use Apalache (SMT-based, bounded) instead of explicit-state TLC. The residual gap and why this matters for an ADRS artifact specifically: TLA+ verifies the spec, not the compiled code, so there's a refinement obligation - show the implementation refines the spec (a refinement mapping / trace inclusion), otherwise you've verified a model the code doesn't match; and liveness results are only as honest as your fairness assumptions. My judgment: an ADRS-produced protocol is exactly where formal verification earns its keep, because the search optimized against a performance proxy and its hidden hold-outs, neither of which constrains all interleavings - the optimizer had every incentive to remove synchronization the benchmarks didn't need, so a benchmark-clean, hold-out-clean artifact is precisely the artifact most likely to hide a rare-interleaving safety bug. I'd gate production on a passing TLA+ spec at a defensible scope plus a refinement argument, and treat 'passes all benchmarks' as necessary but nowhere near sufficient.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Writes the actual Spec = Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness form, gets fairness-for-liveness and lasso/SCC cycle detection right, quantifies state explosion as S^N, gives an ordered mitigation ladder including symmetry reduction and Apalache/TLAPS, and closes with the refinement gap and the sharp original judgment that ADRS artifacts are the highest-value verification targets. Mastery.

criteria: spec vs implementation; TLA+ describes behaviors/states
state explosion is exponential in components/values
verification covers all interleavings testing samples

questions.prompt: On the whiteboard, derive the training-compute rule of thumb C ~ 6ND from first principles. Define N and D precisely, and tell me why inference (forward-only) is roughly 2ND.
probes: Where does the factor of 2 in '2 FLOPs per parameter' come from, and where does the extra 3x for training come from?
Does the 6ND rule count attention FLOPs, and when does that omission matter?

no_hire.answer: C = 6ND is the formula for training compute. N is the model size and D is the data. You multiply them and get FLOPs.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Recites the formula with no derivation. Cannot say where 6 comes from, confuses params with data size, no factor-of-2 reasoning.

weak_hire.answer: N is the number of parameters and D is the number of training tokens. Forward and backward passes cost roughly 2 and 4 units, so together it's 6 times N times D. Inference only does the forward pass so it's about a third, ~2ND.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right shape and gets the 2/4 split and the 2ND inference number, but can't justify the 2 FLOPs per param (multiply + add) or say what N excludes.

hire.answer: N is the non-embedding parameter count, D is the number of training tokens. A matmul against a weight is a multiply-accumulate = 2 FLOPs (one multiply, one add), and each parameter is used once per token in the forward pass, so forward ~ 2ND FLOPs. The backward pass computes gradients w.r.t. both inputs and weights, which is about 2x the forward cost, so ~4ND. Total training ~ 6ND. Inference is forward-only, so ~2ND. The rule ignores attention score FLOPs (the O(seq^2) term) and embedding lookups, so it undercounts at long context.
hire.interviewer_note: Solid: defines N/D correctly, derives the 2-FLOP MAC, the 2x backward, and flags the attention omission. Push for the exact backward accounting and when the seq^2 term breaks the rule.

strong_hire.answer: N = non-embedding params (the matmul weights), D = training tokens. Per token, each weight participates in one multiply-accumulate = 2 FLOPs, and every weight is touched once, so forward = 2ND. Backward is 2x forward because there are two matmuls per layer in the backward pass — the gradient w.r.t. the layer input (to propagate) and the gradient w.r.t. the weights (to update) — each the same cost as the forward matmul, giving 4ND. Sum = 6ND per full training pass over D tokens. Forward-only inference is 2ND. Caveats a staff engineer flags: (1) the rule counts only the dense linear layers, so it excludes the attention score/softmax/value FLOPs which scale as O(n_layers * seq^2 * d) — at short context this is <5% but at 100k+ context attention can dominate and 6ND badly undercounts; (2) it excludes embedding params (they're a lookup, ~2 FLOPs only at the output projection), which is why N is 'non-embedding'; (3) activation recomputation (gradient checkpointing) adds an extra forward, pushing the effective factor toward ~8ND in practice, so 6ND is a lower bound for planning. I use 6ND for compute-budget and scaling-law arithmetic but add the explicit attention term whenever seq * n_layers is large relative to d_model.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full derivation including WHY backward is 2x (two matmuls), precise definition of N, the seq^2 correction with a scale threshold, and the recomputation caveat pushing to 8ND. Principal-level command of the rule and its boundaries.

criteria: N = non-embedding params, D = training tokens
attention/embeddings ignored; matters at long context

questions.prompt: For a single transformer layer, walk me through where the FLOPs actually go — QKV projections, attention scores, output projection, and the FFN. Then tell me at what sequence length the attention's quadratic term starts to dominate.
probes: Write the FLOP count for the attention score matmul vs an FFN matmul.
Given d_model and d_ff = 4*d_model, at what seq length does attention overtake the FFN?

no_hire.answer: Attention is the expensive part because it's quadratic. The FFN is just a couple of linear layers so it's cheap. Most of the compute is in the attention softmax.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Backwards. Believes attention dominates at typical context; can't write a single FLOP count. Common misconception.

weak_hire.answer: The projections (Q, K, V, output) and the FFN are matrix multiplies that scale with sequence length times d_model squared. The attention scores are quadratic in sequence length. So for short sequences the FFN and projections dominate, and for long sequences the quadratic attention takes over.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct qualitative split and the right direction on the crossover, but no explicit FLOP formulas and no estimate of where the crossover actually is.

hire.answer: Per layer, batch 1: QKV projections = 3 * 2 * seq * d_model^2, output projection = 2 * seq * d_model^2 (all O(seq * d^2)). Attention scores QK^T = 2 * seq^2 * d_model and the softmax-weighted value sum = 2 * seq^2 * d_model, so attention is O(seq^2 * d). FFN with d_ff = 4*d_model: up-proj + down-proj = 2 * 2 * seq * d_model * d_ff = 16 * seq * d_model^2, which is the single biggest chunk. Attention's seq^2 term overtakes the projections when seq ~ d_model. So for d_model ~ 4096, attention dominates only past ~4k tokens; below that the FFN is the bulk (~2/3 of the layer).
hire.interviewer_note: Writes the actual formulas, gets FFN as the dominant term, and lands the seq ~ d_model crossover. Strong. Push for the precise crossover including the constant factors and the head-count independence.

strong_hire.answer: Per layer, batch 1, ignoring bias: linear parts scale as seq * d^2. QKV = 6 * seq * d^2, output proj = 2 * seq * d^2, FFN (d_ff = 4d) = 16 * seq * d^2 — total linear = 24 * seq * d^2, of which FFN is 16/24 = 2/3. Attention scores + value aggregation = 4 * seq^2 * d (note it's independent of head count — splitting d across h heads keeps total d fixed). Attention overtakes the linear projections when 4 * seq^2 * d > 24 * seq * d^2, i.e. seq > 6 * d_model. So for d_model = 4096 the quadratic term dominates only past ~24k tokens, not at 4k as people often guess. That's why FlashAttention (removing the materialized n-by-n matrix, making it IO-aware and memory-linear) matters most at long context, and why at typical 2k-8k context the FFN is the throughput bottleneck and the first target for quantization/MoE. Two caveats: (1) with GQA/MQA the KV projection shrinks but the score matmul is unchanged, so the crossover point moves little; (2) causal masking halves the effective score FLOPs but not the asymptotics. The practical upshot: optimize the FFN matmuls for short context, optimize attention IO for long context.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Exact constants, the seq > 6*d_model crossover (not the naive seq ~ d), head-count invariance, and ties it to FlashAttention/MoE/quantization decisions. Mastery of the FLOP budget.

criteria: QKV + output proj are O(seq * d^2)
attention scores QK^T and softmax*V are O(seq^2 * d)
FFN is ~2 * (seq * d * d_ff) and dominates at short ctx
crossover when seq ~ d_model (order of magnitude)
FFN ~2/3 of layer FLOPs at typical ctx

questions.prompt: Derive the KV cache size formula for a decoder transformer, then plug in a 7B model at 8k context, batch 1, FP16. Show me it grows linearly and tell me what that implies for max batch size.
probes: Why is there a factor of 2, and what changes under GQA/MQA?
At 128k context, roughly how much KV memory, and how does that compare to the weights?

no_hire.answer: The KV cache stores the keys and values so the model doesn't recompute them. It's some memory that grows as you generate more tokens. For a 7B model it's a few gigabytes.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Knows the purpose but can't write the formula, guesses the number, no linearity argument or batch implication.

weak_hire.answer: KV cache = 2 (keys and values) times number of layers times number of heads times head dimension times sequence length times batch times bytes per element. It grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, so long contexts and big batches eat memory fast, which limits how many requests you can run at once.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct formula and linearity and the batch implication, but doesn't plug in real numbers or mention GQA reducing n_kv_heads.

hire.answer: KV bytes = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_elem. The 2 is one buffer for keys, one for values. For a 7B model: ~32 layers, d_model = 4096 so n_heads * head_dim = 4096, FP16 = 2 bytes. Per token per layer = 2 * 4096 * 2 = 16 KB, times 32 layers = 512 KB/token. At 8k tokens, batch 1: ~4 GB. It's linear in seq and batch, so 128k context or batch 32 would be ~16x. Since the weights are ~14 GB in FP16, at long context the KV cache rivals or exceeds the weights, and it directly caps batch size on a fixed HBM budget. GQA cuts n_kv_heads (e.g. 8 instead of 32), shrinking KV 4x.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct formula, plugs in the 7B numbers to ~4 GB, shows linearity and the batch cap, and knows GQA. Strong. Push on the exact GQA arithmetic and the serving consequence.

strong_hire.answer: KV bytes = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes. The 2 is keys plus values; n_kv_heads (not n_query_heads) because GQA/MQA share KV across query groups. For Llama-2-7B: 32 layers, 32 heads * 128 head_dim = 4096, MHA so n_kv_heads = 32, FP16. Per-token-per-layer KV = 2 * 4096 * 2 bytes = 16 KB; * 32 layers = 512 KB/token; * 8192 tokens = ~4 GB at batch 1. Weights are ~14 GB, so on an 80 GB A100 you have ~66 GB for KV -> at 8k that's a max batch of ~16 before OOM, and at 32k context (~16 GB/seq) you're down to ~4 concurrent sequences. This linear-in-(seq*batch) growth is the core serving constraint: throughput is gated by how many sequences' KV fit, not by FLOPs. Mitigations, in order of impact: (1) GQA — Llama-3-8B uses 8 KV heads, cutting KV 4x, so ~1 GB at 8k; (2) KV quantization to FP8/INT8, another 2x; (3) PagedAttention to eliminate the 60-80% fragmentation waste of contiguous allocation; (4) sliding-window / attention-sink eviction to bound KV at very long context. The subtle failure mode: naive contiguous max-length pre-allocation reserves for the worst case, so effective batch is far below the arithmetic max — which is exactly what vLLM's paged cache fixes.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Exact formula with the n_kv_heads subtlety, plugs in Llama-specific numbers, derives the concrete batch cap on an A100, and ranks GQA/quantization/paging/eviction by impact plus the fragmentation failure mode. Systems-level mastery.

criteria: 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq * batch * bytes
KV caps batch; GQA shrinks n_kv_heads

questions.prompt: A 7B model fits fine for inference in FP16 on a 24GB card, but training it OOMs on an 80GB card. Derive the full training memory footprint and pinpoint the number people forget.
probes: How much memory does the Adam optimizer state add, and why?
How does mixed precision change the weight/gradient/state accounting?

no_hire.answer: Training needs more memory because you store gradients too. So it's roughly double the weights. 80GB should be enough for a 7B model, so maybe the batch is too big.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Only counts weights + gradients, completely misses optimizer state and activations. Cannot explain a real OOM.

weak_hire.answer: You need memory for the weights, the gradients (same size as weights), the optimizer state, and the activations for backprop. Adam stores extra state per parameter. Activations grow with batch size and sequence length. All together it's several times the model size, which is why training OOMs when inference fits.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Names all four buckets and knows Adam adds state, but doesn't quantify — misses that Adam is 2x and the FP32 master-copy detail in mixed precision.

hire.answer: Four buckets. (1) Weights, (2) gradients — same count as weights, (3) Adam optimizer state — two values per parameter, the first moment m and second moment v, so 2x the weights, (4) activations saved for the backward pass, which scale with batch * seq * n_layers * d_model. The term people forget is the Adam 2x: for a 7B model in FP32 that's 28 GB for weights + 28 GB grads + 56 GB optimizer = 112 GB before a single activation, which is why 80 GB OOMs even though FP16 inference is only ~14 GB. Mitigations: mixed precision, ZeRO/FSDP to shard optimizer state across devices, and gradient checkpointing to trade compute for activation memory.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct four buckets, identifies Adam 2x as the forgotten term, and does the FP32 arithmetic to explain the OOM. Strong. Push on the mixed-precision master-copy accounting and the activation formula.

strong_hire.answer: Total = weights + gradients + optimizer state + activations. Per parameter, the classic FP32 Adam accounting is: weights 4 bytes, gradients 4 bytes, Adam m 4 bytes + v 4 bytes = 16 bytes/param, so a 7B model is ~112 GB before activations — that's why it OOMs on 80 GB even though FP16 inference is ~14 GB. The forgotten number is the Adam 2x (m and v). Mixed-precision training (the standard '16 bytes/param' from the ZeRO paper) is actually MORE subtle: you keep BF16 weights (2) + BF16 grads (2) for the compute, PLUS an FP32 master copy of weights (4) and FP32 Adam m (4) + v (4) = 16 bytes/param total, ~112 GB — mixed precision saves activation memory and speeds matmuls but does NOT shrink this state (the FP32 master copy is needed so tiny updates don't vanish in BF16 rounding). Activations are the fourth bucket and scale as ~batch * seq * n_layers * d_model * bytes * (constant for the intermediate tensors), which dominates at large batch/long seq; gradient checkpointing drops them to O(sqrt(layers)) worth by recomputing in the backward pass (~+33% compute). Real fixes, ranked: (1) ZeRO-1/2/3 or FSDP to shard optimizer/grads/weights across data-parallel ranks — ZeRO-3 divides the 16 bytes/param by the DP degree; (2) gradient checkpointing for activations; (3) 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes) to quantize m/v, cutting the optimizer 4x; (4) offload optimizer state to CPU/NVMe. So the OOM story is: inference = weights only; training = ~8x weights just for the parameter-linear state, before activations.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise byte-level accounting, the mixed-precision FP32-master-copy subtlety (that it does NOT save optimizer memory), the activation scaling and checkpointing tradeoff, and a ranked ZeRO/8-bit-Adam/offload mitigation list. Principal-level.

criteria: the '2x for Adam' is the forgotten term
mixed precision keeps FP32 master copy
activations scale with batch*seq*layers; checkpointing trades compute

questions.prompt: On the whiteboard, given a kernel's FLOPs and the bytes it moves, plus a device with a peak FLOP/s and a memory bandwidth, compute the ridge point and decide whether the kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound. Do it for LLM decode.
probes: What is the ridge-point arithmetic intensity, and which side is decode on?
How does batching move a decode kernel across the roofline?

no_hire.answer: You compare the FLOPs to the bandwidth. If it needs a lot of compute it's compute-bound, otherwise memory-bound. Decode is compute-bound because generating tokens is expensive.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No arithmetic-intensity concept, no ridge point, and wrongly calls decode compute-bound. Fundamental misunderstanding.

weak_hire.answer: Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs divided by bytes moved. The ridge point is where the machine's peak compute equals its bandwidth times intensity. If a kernel's intensity is below the ridge point it's memory-bound, above it it's compute-bound. LLM decode is memory-bound because it reads a lot of weights for little compute. Batching helps.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct definitions, correct ridge-point idea, correct decode verdict, but doesn't compute a number or explain the batching mechanism precisely.

hire.answer: Arithmetic intensity AI = FLOPs / bytes_moved (FLOP per byte). The ridge point is the AI where you saturate compute: AI_ridge = peak_FLOP/s / bandwidth_bytes/s. Below AI_ridge the kernel is memory-bound (limited by bandwidth), above it compute-bound. Example: an A100 has ~312 TFLOP/s (BF16) and ~2 TB/s HBM, so AI_ridge ~ 156 FLOP/byte. LLM decode at batch 1 reads ~2 bytes/param (FP16) and does ~2 FLOP/param, so AI ~ 1 FLOP/byte — far below 156, so decode is deeply memory-bound. Batching amortizes the weight read across B sequences: you read the weights once but do B times the FLOPs, so AI ~ B, and at B ~ 156 you cross the ridge into compute-bound. That's why serving throughput comes from batching, not faster math.
hire.interviewer_note: Computes AI_ridge with real A100 numbers, gets decode's AI ~ 1, and explains batching raising AI to the ridge. Strong. Push on the KV-read term breaking the batching benefit and the prefill contrast.

strong_hire.answer: AI = total_FLOPs / total_bytes_moved from HBM. Ridge point AI* = peak_compute / peak_bandwidth. A100 BF16: 312 TFLOP/s / 2.0 TB/s ~ 156 FLOP/byte; H100: ~990 TFLOP/s / 3.35 TB/s ~ 295 FLOP/byte (the ridge rises as compute outpaces bandwidth, so newer chips are MORE memory-bound for the same kernel). Decode, batch 1: per token you read all N weights (2N bytes in FP16) and do 2N FLOPs, so AI = 2N / 2N = 1 FLOP/byte << 156 -> hard memory-bound, and you realize ~1/156 of peak FLOPs. Batching to B: weights read ONCE, FLOPs scale as 2NB, so AI -> B (up to the ridge at B~156), which is the entire reason we batch. Two things that break the naive story: (1) the KV cache is NOT shared across the batch — each sequence reads its own KV (2 * L * H * d_head * seq bytes), which grows with context and re-lowers AI at long context, so at 32k context batching helps less; (2) prefill is the opposite regime — it processes seq tokens in parallel so AI ~ seq, landing compute-bound, which is why prefill and decode want different optimizations and get disaggregated onto separate pools. Consequences: for decode we optimize bytes (weight quantization to INT4 quarters the weight traffic and quadruples effective AI/throughput; KV quantization; GQA), and we don't bother with faster tensor cores until we're compute-bound. The roofline is the single most useful mental model for deciding where to spend engineering effort.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Ridge point for two devices with the 'newer chips are more memory-bound' insight, exact decode AI derivation, the KV-not-shared caveat that breaks batching at long context, prefill contrast, and the quantization consequence. Definitive systems answer.

criteria: decode AI ~ O(1) per param -> memory-bound
batching raises AI and can cross to compute-bound

questions.prompt: Estimate the single-stream decode throughput (tokens/sec) for a 70B model in FP16 on an H100 with ~3.35 TB/s HBM. Show the memory-bound reasoning, then tell me how batching changes the number.
probes: Why is tokens/sec ~ bandwidth / bytes-read-per-token at batch 1?
What's the throughput ceiling once you batch, and what caps the batch?

no_hire.answer: You'd look at the GPU's FLOP/s and divide by the FLOPs per token. A fast GPU does maybe thousands of tokens per second for a big model.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Uses the compute roofline, which is the wrong bound for decode, and gives an unrealistically high number. Doesn't know decode is memory-bound.

weak_hire.answer: Decode is memory-bound, so the time per token is set by how long it takes to read the weights from HBM. A 70B model in FP16 is about 140 GB, and at 3.35 TB/s that's roughly 0.04 seconds per token, so around 24 tokens per second at batch 1. Batching lets you serve more sequences at once so total throughput goes up.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct memory-bound reasoning and a right-ballpark 24 tok/s, plus the batching direction, but no throughput ceiling or batch cap.

hire.answer: Decode is memory-bound, so per-token latency ~ bytes_read / bandwidth. At batch 1 you read every weight once per token: 70B * 2 bytes = 140 GB. On H100 at 3.35 TB/s: 140/3350 ~ 0.042 s -> ~24 tokens/sec single-stream (before KV reads and overhead, which lower it a bit). Batching doesn't speed up one stream, but since you read the weights once for the whole batch, aggregate throughput scales ~linearly with batch B: at B sequences you get ~24*B tokens/sec until you hit the compute roofline (around B~295 on H100, the ridge point at ~990 TFLOP/s / 3.35 TB/s) or run out of HBM for KV cache. So the batch is capped by whichever comes first — compute-bound saturation or KV memory. INT4 weights would quarter the bytes and roughly quadruple the single-stream number to ~90 tok/s.
hire.interviewer_note: Memory-bound formula, the 24 tok/s number, linear batch scaling with a compute ceiling and KV cap, and the quantization lever. Strong. Push on per-user vs aggregate throughput and the KV-read correction.

strong_hire.answer: Single-stream decode latency is bandwidth-bound: t_token ~ (bytes_read_per_token) / bandwidth. At batch 1, bytes_read ~ model weights (read once) + this sequence's KV cache. Weights: 70B * 2 = 140 GB. On H100 (3.35 TB/s): 140/3350 ~ 42 ms -> ~24 tok/s, minus KV reads and kernel-launch overhead, so realistically ~20 tok/s. Batching: weights are read once and shared across the batch, so per-token wall-clock stays ~constant while you emit B tokens per step -> aggregate ~ 24*B tok/s, but each individual user still sees ~24 tok/s (that's the crucial per-user vs aggregate distinction — batching raises throughput, not per-user speed). The ceiling: aggregate throughput rises with B until AI crosses the ridge (~B=295 for H100 with FP16 weights, matching the ~990 TFLOP/s / 3.35 TB/s ridge point) and you become compute-bound at ~peak FLOP/s / (2 FLOP/param) — OR until KV cache exhausts HBM first. For 70B, weights take 140 GB of a 141 GB H200 / need 2xH100, leaving little for KV, so in practice KV memory caps B well before the compute ridge — meaning tensor/pipeline parallelism across GPUs is required and inter-GPU bandwidth (NVLink) becomes the new bound. Levers: INT4 weight quant (bytes/token /4 -> ~4x single-stream to ~90 tok/s AND frees HBM for larger B), speculative decoding (raises effective tokens per target pass, helping the latency-bound low-batch regime), GQA/KV-quant (more concurrent sequences). The headline serving metric is tokens/sec/GPU at a fixed inter-token-latency SLO, not raw single-stream.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Exact latency formula, ~24 tok/s with overhead correction, the per-user-vs-aggregate distinction, the KV-caps-batch-before-compute-ridge reality for 70B, multi-GPU/NVLink consequence, and the quant/spec-decode/GQA levers plus the right SLO metric. Mastery.

criteria: decode is memory-bound so time ~ bytes-read / bandwidth
batching multiplies aggregate throughput until compute-bound

questions.prompt: Derive the parameter count of a decoder transformer from vocab size, d_model, n_layers, and d_ff — embeddings, attention, and FFN. Then tell me the rule of thumb for which block dominates and why.
probes: Write the per-layer attention and FFN parameter counts.
For d_ff = 4*d_model, what fraction of non-embedding params is the FFN?

no_hire.answer: Parameters come from the layers. You add up all the weight matrices. The embedding is the biggest part because the vocabulary is huge, like 50,000 words.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Can't write any per-layer count and wrongly claims embeddings dominate (only true for tiny models). No FFN-dominance rule.

weak_hire.answer: There's the embedding matrix (vocab times d_model), then each layer has attention weights (the Q, K, V, and output projections, each d_model by d_model) and an FFN with two matrices d_model by d_ff. The FFN is bigger because d_ff is usually 4 times d_model. Total is roughly the per-layer count times the number of layers plus the embeddings.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right components and knows the FFN is bigger, but doesn't consolidate into the 12*n*d^2 rule or give the 2/3 fraction precisely.

hire.answer: Embedding: vocab * d_model (input, often tied with output). Per layer: attention = 4 * d_model^2 for the Q, K, V, and output projections (each d_model x d_model). FFN = 2 * d_model * d_ff; with d_ff = 4*d_model that's 8 * d_model^2. So per layer = 4 + 8 = 12 * d_model^2, and the FFN is 8/12 = 2/3 of the per-layer params. Total non-embedding ~ 12 * n_layers * d_model^2. The rule of thumb: FFN dominates (~2/3) because d_ff is 4x d_model, and the embedding only matters for small models — for large models the 12*n*d^2 term swamps vocab*d_model, which is exactly why N in scaling laws is the non-embedding count. Quick check: d_model=4096, n=32 -> 12*32*4096^2 ~ 6.4B, order-of-magnitude right for a 7B model.
hire.interviewer_note: Full derivation, the 12*n*d^2 consolidation, the 2/3 FFN fraction, embedding-only-matters-for-small-models, and a sanity check. Strong. Push on GQA/MoE corrections and the tied-embedding detail.

strong_hire.answer: Break it into three: (1) Embeddings — input token embedding vocab * d_model, plus output projection vocab * d_model (usually tied, so counted once); positional params are negligible for RoPE (none) vs learned. (2) Attention per layer — W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O each d_model x d_model = 4 * d_model^2 (biases negligible). (3) FFN per layer — up-proj d_model x d_ff + down-proj d_ff x d_model = 2 * d_model * d_ff; with the standard d_ff = 4*d_model that's 8 * d_model^2 (SwiGLU adds a third gate matrix, so it's 3 * d_model * d_ff, often with d_ff tuned to ~8/3*d_model to keep the count constant). Per-layer total = 12 * d_model^2, FFN = 2/3, attention = 1/3. Total non-embedding N ~ 12 * n_layers * d_model^2. This is why: (a) N in C=6ND and in scaling laws is the non-embedding count — the embedding vocab*d_model is O(d) not O(n*d^2), so it's a rounding error for a 70B model but a large fraction for a 125M model (which is why small-model scaling curves need the embedding term); (b) the FFN is the first target for MoE (replace the 2/3 dense FFN with sparse experts to grow params at fixed active FLOPs) and for quantization. Corrections: GQA shrinks W_K and W_V (fewer KV heads) so attention drops slightly below 1/3; MoE multiplies the FFN term by the number of experts for total params while active params stay at the dense count. Sanity check: Llama-2-7B, d_model=4096, n=32 -> 12*32*4096^2 ~ 6.4B non-embedding + ~0.26B embedding (vocab 32k) ~ 6.7B, matching the ~7B name.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Exact per-block counts with tied embeddings and SwiGLU/GQA/MoE corrections, the 2/3 FFN fraction, why N excludes embeddings and when that matters, ties FFN-dominance to MoE/quantization, and a precise Llama-2-7B reconciliation. Principal-level.

criteria: FFN per layer = 2 * d_model * d_ff = 8 * d_model^2

questions.prompt: Walk me through the RLHF pipeline for aligning a language model, then explain reward hacking: give a concrete example of what the policy learns to exploit and how you'd detect it in production.
probes: Where exactly does the KL penalty enter, and what breaks if you remove it?
Is sycophancy a reward-hacking failure, a reward-model coverage failure, or both?

no_hire.answer: You collect human feedback and train the model to maximize it. Reward hacking is when the model games the reward.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Names the pieces with no mechanism. No KL term, no concrete exploit, no detection.

weak_hire.answer: Three stages: supervised fine-tuning, train a reward model on human preference pairs, then optimize the policy with PPO against the reward model. Reward hacking is when the policy finds high-reward outputs the RM scores well but humans dislike.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct pipeline and definition, but no KL regularization, no concrete exploit, no detection strategy.

hire.answer: SFT -> reward model on pairwise preferences (Bradley-Terry) -> PPO with a per-token KL penalty to the SFT reference policy so the policy stays in-distribution for the RM. Reward hacking is Goodhart's law: e.g. the policy learns verbose, confident, list-formatted answers because raters reward those, even when wrong. Detect via held-out human eval drift vs proxy reward, and by watching the KL blow up.
hire.interviewer_note: Solid mechanism, names the KL anchor and a concrete exploit, gives one detection signal. Push: RM uncertainty, distribution shift over training.

strong_hire.answer: Beyond the standard SFT/RM/PPO loop with KL anchoring: reward hacking is overoptimization of an imperfect proxy. The RM is only accurate near the SFT distribution; PPO pushes the policy off-distribution where RM error compounds, so proxy reward keeps rising while true reward turns over (the classic overoptimization curve, roughly sqrt-shaped in KL). Concrete exploits: sycophancy (agreeing with the user's stated belief), length bias, and format gaming. Mitigations: tune the KL coefficient or use adaptive KL targeting, RM ensembles to penalize disagreement (uncertainty as a cost), iterated RLHF with fresh preference data on-policy, and gold human evals on a frozen holdout to catch proxy-true divergence early. I'd also log reward vs KL and alert when reward rises with no gold-eval gain.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Connects reward hacking to overoptimization theory, the proxy-true divergence, RM coverage, and concrete production mitigations. Staff-level.

questions.prompt: DPO has largely displaced PPO for a lot of preference tuning. Derive the intuition for why DPO works without an explicit reward model, and tell me when you'd still reach for PPO.
probes: What is DPO's implicit reward, and what's the reference-model role?
What failure modes does DPO have that online PPO does not?

no_hire.answer: DPO is simpler than PPO and works better, so people use it instead of reinforcement learning.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Preference without any mechanism. No derivation, no tradeoff.

weak_hire.answer: DPO reparameterizes the RLHF objective so you can train directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, no separate reward model or rollouts. It's more stable and cheaper. PPO is better when you have an online reward signal.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct shape and one real tradeoff, but no derivation of the implicit reward and vague on PPO's edge.

hire.answer: The KL-regularized RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy: pi*(y|x) proportional to pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta). Invert it and the reward equals beta*log(pi/pi_ref) plus a partition term that cancels in pairwise differences, so you can fit the policy directly on preference pairs with a logistic loss over the log-ratio. DPO is offline and only as good as its fixed preference data; PPO wins when you want on-policy exploration, a reusable reward model for many policies, or online signals like verifiable rewards.
hire.interviewer_note: Derives the implicit reward and states the offline limitation plus when PPO is preferable. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: DPO comes from the analytic solution to max_pi E[r] - beta*KL(pi||pi_ref): pi* = pi_ref exp(r/beta)/Z. Solving for r gives r = beta log(pi/pi_ref) + beta log Z; in the Bradley-Terry pairwise loss log Z cancels, yielding the DPO loss on the chosen-minus-rejected log-ratio. Practical failure modes: DPO is fully offline so it can't correct distribution shift, it tends to push down the probability of BOTH chosen and rejected (likelihood displacement) which can degrade the SFT distribution, and it's sensitive to noisy/contradictory pairs since there's no RM to average over. I reach for PPO/GRPO when I have verifiable or programmatic rewards (math, code, tool use), need on-policy data to avoid off-distribution staleness, or want one RM to align a family of models. In practice many labs do DPO/IPO for cheap broad alignment then on-policy RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Full derivation, names likelihood displacement and offline staleness, and gives a crisp decision rule including verifiable-reward RL. Principal-level.

questions.prompt: As you push RLHF longer, proxy reward keeps climbing but the model gets worse by human judgment. Explain what's happening and how you'd control it.
probes: How does the KL coefficient trade off alignment vs reward gain?
Would an RM ensemble help, and why?

no_hire.answer: The model is overfitting the reward, so you should train for fewer steps.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Right instinct (stop earlier) but no understanding of why, or of KL.

weak_hire.answer: The reward model is a proxy; optimizing it too hard makes the policy exploit its errors (Goodhart). Adding a KL penalty to the reference keeps the policy from drifting too far. You can also stop early.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Names Goodhart and KL, but treats them qualitatively with no notion of the reward-KL curve or RM coverage.

hire.answer: It's overoptimization: the RM is accurate near the SFT distribution but errs off-distribution, and PPO drives the policy exactly into those high-RM-error regions, so proxy reward rises while true reward turns over. The KL penalty bounds how far the policy moves; gold reward typically scales like a function of sqrt(KL) then degrades. Controls: tune/adaptively target KL, early-stop on a frozen human/gold eval, and use RM ensembles so disagreement penalizes off-distribution outputs.
hire.interviewer_note: Names the divergence mechanism, the KL budget, and concrete controls. Solid.

strong_hire.answer: Overoptimization is Goodhart on a learned proxy. Empirically (Gao et al.) gold reward as a function of KL distance follows d(alpha - beta*log d)-type curves: it improves then declines, and the turnover point and severity scale with RM size and preference-data size. The lever is the KL budget: small beta lets the policy travel far and exploit RM error, large beta keeps it honest but caps gains. I'd (1) target a KL band with adaptive KL control rather than a fixed coefficient, (2) use an RM ensemble and penalize variance so the policy is pushed away from regions where RMs disagree (epistemic uncertainty as cost), (3) refresh preference data on-policy so the RM stays calibrated where the policy now lives, and (4) gate releases on a frozen gold human eval, alerting when proxy reward rises without gold gain. I'd also consider reward model distillation and label-noise-robust RM training to widen the accurate region.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Quantitative law, uncertainty-as-cost, on-policy RM refresh, and release gating. Research-lead depth.

questions.prompt: You have a fixed compute budget of ~1e23 FLOPs. Use scaling laws to decide model size and training tokens, and tell me where this reasoning breaks down.
probes: What did Chinchilla change relative to the earlier Kaplan picture?
Why might you deliberately train a 'too-small' model past compute-optimal?

no_hire.answer: Bigger models are better, so I'd train the largest model the compute allows.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No notion of token-parameter tradeoff or compute-optimality.

weak_hire.answer: Scaling laws say loss falls as a power law in parameters and data. Chinchilla showed you should scale data and parameters together, roughly 20 tokens per parameter. With 1e23 FLOPs I'd pick N and D so they're balanced.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Knows the 20:1 heuristic and power law, but doesn't use C~6ND to actually solve or discuss limits.

hire.answer: Compute is about C = 6ND. Chinchilla's compute-optimal point puts roughly 20 tokens per parameter, so I solve 6ND = 1e23 with D ~ 20N: that gives N on the order of low-tens of billions of params and D in the hundreds of billions to ~trillion tokens. Caveat: scaling laws predict pretraining loss, which correlates imperfectly with downstream task performance, and they ignore inference cost.
hire.interviewer_note: Uses 6ND, solves it, and flags the loss-vs-downstream gap. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Using C=6ND and Chinchilla's joint fit (optimal N and D both scale like C^0.5), 1e23 FLOPs lands near ~20B params and ~400-500B tokens at the compute-optimal point. But compute-optimal is the wrong objective if you'll serve the model a lot: inference cost is dominated by N, so for a heavily-served model you deliberately go past Chinchilla-optimal in tokens to shrink N (the Llama strategy) and pay more training to save far more inference. Where it breaks: scaling laws fit smooth pretraining loss, but downstream benchmarks can be emergent/discontinuous and only loosely tied to loss; data quality and repetition (epoching) shift the curves; and the laws assume a fixed architecture/optimizer. I'd fit my own law on small proxy runs rather than trust published constants.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Solves it, distinguishes train-optimal from inference-optimal, and critiques the laws' assumptions. Principal-level.

questions.prompt: Explain why frontier models use sparse Mixture-of-Experts, and the main engineering problems MoE introduces.
probes: What is the load-balancing problem and how is it addressed?
Why is MoE memory-heavy even though each token uses few experts?

no_hire.answer: MoE uses multiple models and picks the best one for each input, so it's smarter.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Misconception: experts aren't separate models and there's no 'best one' selection.

weak_hire.answer: MoE replaces the FFN with many expert FFNs and a router that sends each token to the top-k experts. This gives more parameters without more compute per token. The hard part is balancing load across experts.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct mechanism and the key benefit, plus names load balancing. Lacks comms/memory and routing detail.

hire.answer: MoE decouples parameter count from FLOPs per token: a router sends each token to top-k of E experts (e.g. 2 of 64), so capacity grows with E while compute stays ~constant. Problems: load imbalance (a few experts get all tokens) needs an auxiliary load-balancing loss and capacity factors with token dropping; all-to-all communication to route tokens across devices is a bottleneck; and you must hold ALL experts in memory even though each token touches few, so memory scales with total params.
hire.interviewer_note: Names decoupling, routing, aux loss, all-to-all, and the memory point. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: MoE buys parameter scaling at fixed FLOPs/token by replacing dense FFNs with E experts and top-k routing. Engineering issues: (1) Load balancing - without an auxiliary loss (or loss-free bias tricks like DeepSeek's) routing collapses to a few experts; capacity factor + token dropping bound per-expert load but drop tokens under skew. (2) Communication - expert parallelism needs two all-to-alls per MoE layer; at scale this dominates, driving expert-parallel + tensor-parallel topologies and overlap with compute. (3) Memory - all experts must be resident, so a model with 8x the params at the same active FLOPs needs ~8x the weight memory and HBM bandwidth, which is why serving MoE is memory-bound. (4) Training instability - router z-loss to keep logits bounded, and fine-tuning is finicky because routing distributions shift. Tradeoff vs dense: MoE wins on quality-per-training-FLOP but loses on memory footprint and serving complexity, so it pays off mainly at large scale with high request volume.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Covers routing collapse, comms topology, memory-bound serving, stability tricks, and the dense-vs-sparse economics. Research-engineer depth.

questions.prompt: Walk me through what dominates LLM inference cost and latency at serving time, and how systems like PagedAttention and continuous batching help.
probes: Why is decode memory-bandwidth-bound while prefill is compute-bound?
What does PagedAttention fix that static KV allocation got wrong?

no_hire.answer: You put the model on a GPU and batch requests together to go faster.
no_hire.interviewer_note: No prefill/decode distinction, no KV cache, no memory reasoning.

weak_hire.answer: The KV cache stores past keys and values so you don't recompute attention each step; it grows with sequence length and eats memory. Batching requests improves throughput, and continuous batching lets new requests join without waiting for the whole batch to finish.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Knows KV cache and continuous batching, but not the prefill/decode compute profile or PagedAttention's mechanism.

hire.answer: Two phases: prefill processes the prompt in parallel and is compute-bound; decode generates one token at a time and is memory-bandwidth-bound because each step reads the whole KV cache and weights for tiny compute. KV cache size = 2 * layers * heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * dtype, so it dominates memory and caps batch size. Continuous batching keeps the GPU full by adding/removing sequences per step. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed blocks like virtual memory pages, eliminating the fragmentation and over-reservation of contiguous per-request allocation, so you fit far more concurrent sequences.
hire.interviewer_note: Clean prefill/decode split, KV sizing, and what PagedAttention fixes. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Decode arithmetic intensity is terrible: per token you read all weights and the full KV cache to produce one token, so you're bound by HBM bandwidth, not FLOPs - which is why throughput comes from batching (amortizing weight reads) not faster math, and why MoE/large models are memory-bound. Prefill is the opposite, compute-bound and parallel over prompt tokens, which is why TTFT and inter-token latency have different optimizations and people split prefill/decode onto different pools (disaggregated serving). KV cache grows linearly in context and dominates memory; static contiguous allocation wastes 60-80% to internal+external fragmentation and forces conservative max-length reservations. PagedAttention pages KV into blocks with a block table, enabling near-zero waste, copy-on-write sharing for beam search / shared prefixes, and much higher concurrency. Stack the wins: continuous batching + paged KV + chunked prefill to interleave prefill and decode, plus speculative decoding to raise decode arithmetic intensity. The headline metric is tokens/sec/GPU at a TTFT/ITL SLO.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Arithmetic-intensity reasoning, disaggregation, prefix sharing, chunked prefill, and the right serving metric. Systems-level mastery.

questions.prompt: Explain speculative decoding. A 7B draft proposes k=5 tokens for a 70B target; on average 3 are accepted. What's the speedup, and when does it stop helping?
probes: Why is the output distribution provably unchanged?
How does acceptance rate depend on draft-target agreement and temperature?

no_hire.answer: A small model writes a draft and the big model checks it, which is faster.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Gist only; no exactness argument, no speedup reasoning, no limits.

weak_hire.answer: A cheap draft model proposes several tokens, the target verifies them in one forward pass, and accepted tokens are kept. With 3 of 5 accepted you get roughly 3-4 tokens per target step instead of 1, so a ~3x-ish speedup, minus draft overhead.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right mechanism and ballpark speedup, but hand-wavy on exactness and on when it fails.

hire.answer: Draft autoregressively proposes k tokens; the target scores all k+1 positions in one pass; a modified rejection-sampling rule accepts a prefix and resamples the first rejected token from an adjusted distribution, so the output distribution is provably identical to sampling from the target. With ~3 accepted per cycle you produce ~4 tokens (3 + 1 resampled) per target pass, so ~3-4x fewer target passes; net speedup is lower after the draft's own cost. It stops helping when acceptance is low (draft and target disagree, e.g. high temperature or hard domains) or when you're already compute-bound from large batches, because the target pass is no longer cheap relative to throughput.
hire.interviewer_note: Exactness via rejection sampling, correct token accounting, and real limits. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: Speculative decoding trades extra compute for fewer sequential target steps. The draft samples k tokens; the target does one parallel verification; the rejection rule accepts token i with prob min(1, p_target/p_draft) and on rejection resamples from the normalized positive part of (p_target - p_draft), which makes the marginal exactly the target distribution - no quality loss. Token accounting: 3 accepted + 1 free resample = 4 tokens per target pass, ~4x reduction in target passes, but the realized wall-clock speedup is (expected accepted+1)/(1 + c) where c is draft cost relative to target; with a 7B/70B pair c is small so you keep most of it. It degrades when: acceptance drops (temperature up, distribution shift, long reasoning where draft and target diverge), or when the batch is large enough that the target forward is already bandwidth-saturated so the 'free' parallel verification isn't free anymore - speculative decoding mainly helps the low-batch, latency-bound regime. Extensions: self-speculation / Medusa heads remove the separate draft, and tree/multi-candidate drafting raises expected acceptance.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Exact rejection rule, realized-speedup formula, batch-regime caveat, and Medusa/tree extensions. Research depth.

criteria: breaks under low acceptance / large batch

questions.prompt: You need to serve a 70B model cheaply. Talk me through quantization options, what actually degrades quality, and how methods like GPTQ/AWQ avoid it.
probes: What are activation outliers and why do they matter?
Weight-only vs weight+activation quantization - when each?

no_hire.answer: Quantization makes weights smaller by using fewer bits, which saves memory and is faster.
no_hire.interviewer_note: True but generic; no failure modes, no method understanding.

weak_hire.answer: You cast weights to INT8 or INT4 to cut memory and bandwidth, which speeds up the memory-bound decode. Aggressive quantization hurts accuracy, so methods like GPTQ calibrate on data to minimize the error.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Right framing and names GPTQ, but no outlier story or weight-vs-activation distinction.

hire.answer: Since decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, shrinking weights from FP16 to INT8/INT4 directly speeds it up and lets larger models fit. The catch is activation outliers: a few channels have huge magnitudes that, if naively quantized, blow up error - this is why W8A8 is hard. Weight-only methods (GPTQ does error-compensating per-column rounding; AWQ scales salient weight channels by activation statistics) keep activations in FP16 and quantize weights to 4-bit with small accuracy loss. For 70B I'd start with 4-bit weight-only (AWQ/GPTQ) and reserve W8A8 for throughput-critical paths with outlier handling.
hire.interviewer_note: Connects to bandwidth, names outliers, distinguishes weight-only vs W8A8, and gives a concrete plan. Strong.

strong_hire.answer: The win is bandwidth: decode reads weights every token, so 4-bit weights ~ 4x less weight traffic and big throughput gains; it also frees HBM for KV cache / larger batch. Quality loss comes mainly from activation outliers - emergent large-magnitude features in specific channels that dominate the dynamic range; LLM.int8() handles them with mixed-precision decomposition, SmoothQuant migrates outlier scale from activations into weights to enable W8A8, GPTQ does second-order (OBQ-style) error-compensating quantization column by column, and AWQ protects salient channels identified by activation magnitude. Decision: weight-only INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ) is the default for memory-bound single-stream serving with minimal degradation; W8A8 (SmoothQuant) helps when you're compute-bound at high batch and want INT8 tensor cores; KV-cache quantization (FP8/INT8) is increasingly important since KV often dominates memory at long context. I'd validate with perplexity AND task evals (perplexity hides reasoning regressions) and watch for degradation concentrated in long-context or code.
